questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A metaphor is a figure of speech that
options: compares two things using 'like' or 'as'
gives human qualities to non-human things
uses exaggeration for emphasis
describes one thing as being another, without using 'like' or 'as'
questions.explanation: A metaphor makes a direct, implicit comparison by stating one thing is another (e.g., 'the world is a stage'), unlike a simile, which uses 'like' or 'as'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A simile is a figure of speech that compares two unlike things using
options: onomatopoeia only
personification
'like' or 'as'
hyperbole only
questions.explanation: A simile makes an explicit comparison between two different things, signalled by the connecting words 'like' or 'as' (e.g., 'as brave as a lion').

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Personification is a literary device in which
options: a part is used to represent the whole
two contrasting ideas are placed side by side
an exaggerated statement is made for effect
human qualities or actions are attributed to non-human things or abstract ideas
questions.explanation: Personification gives human characteristics (thoughts, feelings, actions) to inanimate objects, animals, or abstract concepts, such as 'the wind whispered'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Hyperbole is a literary device that involves
options: the use of a word that imitates a sound
understatement for ironic effect
a contradiction between two words placed together
deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or dramatic effect
questions.explanation: Hyperbole intentionally overstates something to create emphasis or a strong impression, not intended to be taken literally, e.g., 'I've told you a million times.'

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Irony, as a literary device, refers to a situation in which
options: human traits are given to non-human things
a statement is deliberately made more extreme than reality
there is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens or is meant
a sound is imitated through word choice
questions.explanation: Irony highlights a gap between appearance and reality, expectation and outcome, or literal and intended meaning, often creating a sense of surprise or critique.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Dramatic irony occurs when
options: the audience knows something important that a character in the story does not know
an event happens that is the opposite of what was expected by everyone, including the audience
a character says the exact opposite of what they mean
two words with opposite meanings are placed side by side
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony creates tension or humour because the audience possesses information a character lacks, making the character's words or actions carry additional meaning.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A soliloquy, common in Shakespearean drama, is best described as
options: a stage direction describing the setting
a conversation between two or more characters
a speech in which a character, alone on stage, reveals their inner thoughts to the audience
a song performed by a chorus
questions.explanation: A soliloquy allows a character to express private thoughts and feelings directly to the audience, as though thinking aloud, typically while alone on stage.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An aside, in drama, refers to
options: a brief remark made by a character directly to the audience, unheard by other characters on stage
the main climax of a play
a stage direction indicating the time period
a long speech delivered to all characters present
questions.explanation: An aside is a short comment a character makes that is understood to be heard by the audience but not by the other characters present in the scene.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Tragedy, as a literary genre, typically involves
options: a protagonist whose downfall results from a fatal flaw or a combination of circumstances beyond their control
a purely factual, non-fictional account of events
a lighthearted plot that always ends happily
a series of unconnected short poems
questions.explanation: Classical tragedy centres on a protagonist (often of high status) whose serious flaw or unfortunate circumstances lead to their downfall, evoking pity and fear in the audience.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A tragic hero's downfall is often attributed to a personal flaw known as
options: hamartia
hubris only, and never any other flaw
anagnorisis
catharsis
questions.explanation: Hamartia refers to the tragic hero's inherent flaw or error in judgement that sets in motion the chain of events leading to their downfall.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Catharsis, a concept from Aristotle's theory of tragedy, refers to the
options: final scene of any dramatic work
emotional release or purification experienced by the audience after watching a tragedy
moment a character recognises the truth about their situation
resolution of the main conflict in a comedy
questions.explanation: Catharsis describes the emotional cleansing or release of pity and fear that Aristotle believed audiences experience by witnessing the events of a tragedy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A protagonist in a literary work is best described as
options: the narrator of the story only
a minor character with little influence on the plot
the character who opposes the main character
the central character around whom the main action of the story revolves
questions.explanation: The protagonist is the principal character whose goals, conflicts, and development typically drive the central plot of a literary work.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An antagonist in a literary work is best described as
options: a character who narrates the events of the story
the central character of the story
the character or force that opposes the protagonist
the setting in which the story takes place
questions.explanation: The antagonist creates conflict by opposing the protagonist's goals or desires, driving much of the tension in the plot.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Setting, as an element of a literary work, refers to the
options: time and place in which the events of the story occur
sequence of events in the plot
central message or lesson of the story
list of characters involved in the story
questions.explanation: Setting establishes the historical period, geographical location, and social context within which a narrative's events unfold.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Theme, in literature, refers to the
options: list of characters appearing in the story
physical location where the story is set
sequence of events that make up the plot
central idea, message, or underlying meaning explored in a literary work
questions.explanation: A theme is the deeper, often universal, idea or insight a literary work explores or comments on, distinct from the literal plot events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Plot, as an element of a literary work, refers to the
options: time and place in which the story occurs
structured sequence of events that make up the story
individual characters who appear in the story
moral lesson conveyed by the story
questions.explanation: Plot is the organised arrangement of events and actions in a narrative, typically involving exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Characterisation refers to the
options: rhyme scheme used in a poem
methods a writer uses to develop and reveal a character's personality and traits
central theme explored by the author
physical setting of the literary work
questions.explanation: Characterisation encompasses the techniques (dialogue, action, description, other characters' reactions) an author uses to construct and reveal a character to the reader.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A flat character in a literary work is one who
options: always serves as the story's protagonist
narrates the events of the story
is simple, one-dimensional, and does not undergo significant development
changes and develops significantly throughout the story
questions.explanation: Flat characters are relatively simple, often defined by a single dominant trait, and typically do not undergo the depth of development seen in more complex, rounded characters.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A round character in a literary work is one who
options: appears only briefly in a single scene
is complex, multi-dimensional, and often undergoes significant development
is simple and unchanging throughout the story
exists purely to narrate the events of the plot
questions.explanation: Round characters possess complex, realistic personalities and often evolve meaningfully in response to the story's events, unlike simpler flat characters.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In poetry, a stanza refers to a
options: group of lines forming a unit, similar to a paragraph in prose
specific type of rhyme scheme only
single word repeated at the end of consecutive lines
type of dramatic monologue
questions.explanation: A stanza is a grouped set of lines within a poem, functioning structurally in a similar way to a paragraph in prose writing.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Alliteration is a literary device involving the
options: use of a word that imitates the sound it describes
repetition of an entire line at intervals throughout a poem
repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words
direct comparison of two things using 'like' or 'as'
questions.explanation: Alliteration repeats the same consonant sound at the beginning of neighbouring words (e.g., 'the wild wind whispered'), often used for rhythm and emphasis.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Onomatopoeia is a literary device in which a word
options: is repeated for emphasis at the end of a line
imitates or suggests the natural sound it describes
compares two unlike things using 'like' or 'as'
gives human traits to an inanimate object
questions.explanation: Onomatopoeic words (e.g., 'buzz', 'clang', 'hiss') mimic the actual sound associated with the thing they describe, adding sensory vividness to writing.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A symbol, in literature, is an object, person, or event that
options: represents a deeper meaning beyond its literal sense
always refers exclusively to a religious concept
has no significance beyond its literal, physical presence
only appears in poetry, never in prose or drama
questions.explanation: A symbol carries meaning beyond its literal identity, standing in for a broader idea, theme, or concept within a literary work, such as a dove symbolising peace.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Foreshadowing, as a narrative technique, involves
options: revealing the full ending of a story at its very beginning
giving hints or clues earlier in a story about events that will happen later
using dialogue exclusively to develop the plot
describing a character's physical appearance in detail
questions.explanation: Foreshadowing plants subtle clues or hints about future plot developments, building anticipation or tension without fully revealing what is to come.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A flashback, as a narrative technique, involves
options: interrupting the present action of a story to depict an earlier event
combining two separate stories into a single narrative
predicting future events before they occur
describing the setting of a story in great detail
questions.explanation: A flashback shifts the narrative back in time from the current point in the story, often providing background information or context relevant to present events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Comedy, as a literary genre, is typically characterised by
options: a purely factual, non-fictional account of real events
a light-hearted tone and a resolution that is generally happy or favourable for the main characters
the complete absence of any conflict or tension
a serious tone ending in the protagonist's downfall or death
questions.explanation: Comedy typically employs humour and wit, often involving misunderstandings or obstacles that are ultimately resolved happily, contrasting with the serious, often fatal, outcomes of tragedy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A narrator who tells a story using pronouns such as 'he', 'she', and 'they', without being a character in the story, is described as using
options: first-person narration
third-person narration
dramatic narration
second-person narration
questions.explanation: Third-person narration recounts events from outside the story using external pronouns, unlike first-person narration, which uses 'I' and involves a narrator who is also a character.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Antony and Cleopatra, a play prescribed on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: J.B. Priestley
Efua Sutherland
William Shakespeare
Robert Bolt
questions.explanation: Antony and Cleopatra is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, based on the historical relationship between the Roman general Mark Antony and the Egyptian queen Cleopatra.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Antony and Cleopatra, Mark Antony is a Roman general who is romantically involved with
options: Octavia, sister of Octavius Caesar, exclusively
Enobarbus's wife
Charmian, Cleopatra's attendant
Cleopatra, the Queen of Egypt
questions.explanation: The central relationship of the play is the passionate romantic and political alliance between Antony and Cleopatra, which conflicts with Antony's duties as a Roman leader.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Antony and Cleopatra, Antony forms a political alliance with Rome (the Second Triumvirate) alongside Octavius Caesar and
options: Enobarbus
Pompey
Agrippa
Lepidus
questions.explanation: The Second Triumvirate in the play consists of Mark Antony, Octavius Caesar, and Lepidus, ruling different parts of the Roman world.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Antony and Cleopatra, Antony marries Octavia mainly in an attempt to
options: gain the throne of Egypt through marriage
escape from Cleopatra's influence permanently
strengthen and cement his political alliance with her brother, Octavius Caesar
please the citizens of Alexandria
questions.explanation: Antony's marriage to Octavia is primarily a political move intended to reconcile and solidify his fragile alliance with Octavius Caesar, though it ultimately fails when Antony returns to Cleopatra.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Enobarbus, a key supporting character in Antony and Cleopatra, is best described as
options: a loyal friend and soldier to Antony who eventually deserts him
Cleopatra's brother
the ruler of Rome
Antony's chief political rival
questions.explanation: Enobarbus is Antony's loyal companion for much of the play, but he eventually abandons Antony for Octavius Caesar's side, later dying of grief over his betrayal.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The famous description of Cleopatra's barge, describing her as an image where 'age cannot wither her, nor custom stale her infinite variety,' is delivered by
options: Octavius Caesar
Antony
Enobarbus
Charmian
questions.explanation: Enobarbus delivers this celebrated description of Cleopatra's magnetic and endlessly captivating charm to fellow Romans, capturing her legendary allure.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Antony and Cleopatra, the naval battle at Actium is significant because
options: it is fought entirely on land rather than at sea
Antony suffers a decisive defeat after following Cleopatra's fleet as it retreats
it results in a decisive victory that secures Antony's control over Rome
it takes place after Antony's death
questions.explanation: The Battle of Actium marks a critical turning point: Antony's forces are defeated after he follows Cleopatra's retreating ships, severely damaging his military and political standing.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: At the end of Antony and Cleopatra, Antony dies by
options: falling on his own sword after mistakenly believing Cleopatra is dead
drowning during the Battle of Actium
being executed by Octavius Caesar's soldiers
being poisoned by Cleopatra
questions.explanation: Antony, believing a false report that Cleopatra has died, attempts suicide by falling on his sword, dying shortly afterward in Cleopatra's monument.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Cleopatra's death at the end of the play is caused by
options: a fatal wound suffered in battle
the bite of an asp (venomous snake) that she deliberately allows to bite her
poison administered by Octavius Caesar
natural causes after a long illness
questions.explanation: Cleopatra chooses to die with dignity by allowing an asp, smuggled to her in a basket of figs, to bite her, rather than be paraded as a captive in Octavius Caesar's triumph in Rome.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A major theme explored in Antony and Cleopatra is the conflict between
options: urban and rural life
science and religion
youth and old age exclusively
romantic passion and political duty/responsibility
questions.explanation: The play's central tension arises from Antony being torn between his overwhelming love for Cleopatra and the political and military obligations of his role as a Roman leader.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The Marriage of Anansewa, a play on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: Efua Sutherland
Robert Bolt
Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan
Wole Soyinka
questions.explanation: The Marriage of Anansewa is a well-known play by the Ghanaian playwright Efua Sutherland, drawing on the Anansegoro (Ananse storytelling) tradition.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In The Marriage of Anansewa, the central character Ananse is best described as a
options: foreign trader visiting the village
cunning and resourceful father scheming to secure wealth through his daughter's marriage
wealthy chief with no financial troubles
young suitor seeking Anansewa's hand in marriage
questions.explanation: Ananse is a trickster figure, drawing on the traditional Ananse (spider) folklore character, who schemes to profit from arranging his daughter Anansewa's marriage to multiple wealthy suitors simultaneously.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In The Marriage of Anansewa, Ananse's scheme involves
options: giving away his daughter for free to the poorest suitor
arranging a marriage without asking for any dowry
refusing all suitors who ask for his daughter's hand
promising his daughter Anansewa in marriage to several wealthy chiefs at the same time to extract gifts from each
questions.explanation: Ananse's central trick is accepting proposals and gifts from multiple wealthy chiefs simultaneously, intending to eventually choose just one, exploiting the others for material gain.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The character Anansewa, in The Marriage of Anansewa, is best described as
options: a rival trickster figure to Ananse
Ananse's wife, who supports his scheming
a foreign princess visiting Ananse's village
Ananse's daughter, whose marriage is used as a pawn in her father's scheme
questions.explanation: Anansewa is Ananse's daughter, whose feelings and wellbeing are largely subordinated to her father's elaborate financial scheme involving her marriage prospects.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A major theme explored in The Marriage of Anansewa is
options: the industrial revolution and its effects on rural life
greed and the exploitation of family relationships for material gain
the discovery of a hidden natural resource
war between two rival nations
questions.explanation: The play critiques Ananse's greedy manipulation of his own daughter's marriage prospects purely for personal financial benefit, exploring themes of deception and exploitation.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The dramatic style of The Marriage of Anansewa draws heavily on the Ghanaian storytelling tradition known as
options: Kabuki
Anansegoro
Commedia dell'arte
Greek tragedy
questions.explanation: Anansegoro is a Ghanaian theatrical tradition derived from Ananse (spider) trickster folktales, and Efua Sutherland adapted this storytelling style into a formal dramatic structure in the play.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Once Upon an Elephant, an alternative African drama text on the JAMB syllabus, was written by
options: Wole Soyinka
Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan
Efua Sutherland
J.B. Priestley
questions.explanation: Once Upon an Elephant is a Nigerian play by Bosede Ademilua-Afolayan, offered as an alternative African drama text alongside The Marriage of Anansewa on the harmonized syllabus.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Once Upon an Elephant, as an African drama text, generally engages with themes relating to
options: European industrial history
African cultural heritage, tradition, and societal values
Antarctic exploration
space travel and futuristic technology
questions.explanation: As with much African drama on the syllabus, the play engages with themes of cultural heritage and tradition, reflecting concerns central to African dramatic literature.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A Man for All Seasons, a play on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: Robert Bolt
William Shakespeare
J.B. Priestley
Efua Sutherland
questions.explanation: A Man for All Seasons is a historical drama by the English playwright Robert Bolt, depicting the life and principled stand of Sir Thomas More.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A Man for All Seasons centres on the life of
options: a fictional English merchant with no historical basis
King Henry VIII himself as the main protagonist
Queen Elizabeth I of England
Sir Thomas More, who refuses to support King Henry VIII's divorce and remarriage
questions.explanation: The play dramatises the true story of Sir Thomas More, who was ultimately executed for refusing to endorse King Henry VIII's break from the Catholic Church to remarry.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of A Man for All Seasons is
options: the exploration of unknown territories overseas
romantic love overcoming social class barriers
individual conscience and moral integrity in the face of political pressure
the industrialisation of English society
questions.explanation: The play explores Thomas More's unwavering commitment to his personal and religious conscience, even at the cost of his life, when pressured by the King to compromise his principles.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In A Man for All Seasons, the character called 'The Common Man' functions mainly as
options: King Henry VIII's most trusted advisor
the play's chief antagonist
a narrator and commentator who plays several minor roles throughout the play
Thomas More's son
questions.explanation: The Common Man serves as a versatile narrator figure, addressing the audience directly and taking on multiple minor roles, providing commentary on the unfolding events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: At the end of A Man for All Seasons, Sir Thomas More is
options: exiled from England permanently
pardoned and restored to his position as Chancellor
reconciled with King Henry VIII
executed for treason after refusing to take the Oath of Supremacy
questions.explanation: More is ultimately convicted and executed for treason after steadfastly refusing to swear the Oath of Supremacy, which would have required him to recognise the King's authority over the Church.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An Inspector Calls, a play on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: J.B. Priestley
Harper Lee
William Shakespeare
Robert Bolt
questions.explanation: An Inspector Calls is a play by the English playwright J.B. Priestley, exploring themes of social responsibility through the mysterious investigation of a young woman's death.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In An Inspector Calls, the character Inspector Goole visits the Birling family to investigate the
options: murder of a local business rival
suicide of a young working-class woman named Eva Smith
disappearance of the Birlings' youngest son
theft of valuable family jewellery
questions.explanation: Inspector Goole arrives to question the Birling family about their individual roles in the events leading to the suicide of Eva Smith, a young working-class woman.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of An Inspector Calls is
options: the benefits of unregulated capitalism
the joys of family reconciliation
collective social responsibility and the consequences of individual actions on others
the exploration of space and time travel
questions.explanation: Priestley uses the play to argue that individuals bear responsibility for the wellbeing of others in society, critiquing selfish, class-based indifference to the suffering of the less fortunate.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: At the end of An Inspector Calls, it is revealed that
options: Inspector Goole was definitively proven to be a real police officer
Eva Smith was found alive and unharmed
the entire investigation was immediately dismissed as irrelevant by the family
Inspector Goole's true identity and the true sequence of events remain deliberately ambiguous, adding a supernatural or moral dimension to the play
questions.explanation: The play's ending leaves open questions about whether Inspector Goole was a real inspector, a moral device, or something supernatural, reinforcing its central message about responsibility regardless of the literal explanation.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An Inspector Calls is notable for its use of dramatic structure that unfolds in
options: multiple settings across several different countries
an entirely wordless, mime-based performance style
real time, largely within a single setting (the Birling family's dining room)
a non-linear structure jumping between many decades
questions.explanation: The play largely adheres to the classical unities, unfolding in continuous real time within essentially one setting, heightening the tension of the investigation.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: So the Path Does Not Die, a novel on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: Pede Hollist
Elma Shaw
Harper Lee
Susanne Bellefeuille
questions.explanation: So the Path Does Not Die is a novel by the Sierra Leonean-American writer Pede Hollist.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: So the Path Does Not Die is primarily set in which West African country?
options: Nigeria
Sierra Leone
Ghana
Senegal
questions.explanation: The novel is set primarily in Sierra Leone, drawing on the author's own Sierra Leonean background and cultural context.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central concern of So the Path Does Not Die relates to
options: a European colonial administrator's diary
a war between two rival West African kingdoms
the discovery of oil reserves in a coastal village
the impact of a harmful traditional practice on the life of its central female character
questions.explanation: The novel engages with the lasting personal and psychological impact of a harmful traditional practice on its central female protagonist, exploring themes of tradition, trauma, and identity.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A major theme in So the Path Does Not Die is the tension between
options: traditional cultural practices and individual autonomy or modern values
science fiction and futuristic technology
monarchy and democracy in a fictional kingdom
urban development and environmental conservation
questions.explanation: The novel explores the conflict between deeply rooted traditional expectations and the protagonist's own sense of self and desire to define her own path in life.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Redemption Road, a novel on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: Harper Lee
Pede Hollist
Elma Shaw
Robert Bolt
questions.explanation: Redemption Road is a novel by the Liberian writer Elma Shaw.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Redemption Road is primarily set against the backdrop of
options: the industrial revolution in Britain
ancient Egyptian civilisation
modern-day Wall Street finance
civil conflict and its aftermath in Liberia
questions.explanation: The novel is set in Liberia and engages with the lasting effects of the Liberian civil conflict on individuals and communities.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of Redemption Road is
options: the history of transatlantic shipping routes
healing, reconciliation, and rebuilding in the aftermath of conflict
the rivalry between two European royal families
space exploration and scientific discovery
questions.explanation: As its title suggests, the novel centrally explores paths toward personal and communal healing and reconciliation following the trauma of civil conflict.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Both So the Path Does Not Die and Redemption Road, as African prose texts on the JAMB syllabus, share a common concern with
options: depicting purely fictional fantasy worlds unconnected to reality
chronicling the history of European exploration of Africa
exploring difficult social realities in West Africa and their impact on individual characters
describing life in wealthy, conflict-free societies
questions.explanation: Both novels engage seriously with real, difficult social and historical realities in West Africa (harmful traditional practices and civil conflict, respectively) and their profound effects on individual lives.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Pede Hollist and Elma Shaw, the authors of the two prescribed African prose texts, are both writers connected to
options: Northern Europe with no African connection
West Africa, drawing on their personal or ancestral connections to the region in their fiction
South America, with no connection to West Africa
Southeast Asia exclusively
questions.explanation: Both authors have personal ties to West Africa (Sierra Leone and Liberia respectively), and their prescribed novels draw significantly on the social and historical realities of that region.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: To Kill a Mockingbird, one of the prescribed non-African prose texts, was written by
options: Susanne Bellefeuille
Harper Lee
Robert Bolt
J.B. Priestley
questions.explanation: To Kill a Mockingbird is a celebrated novel by the American author Harper Lee, first published in 1960.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: To Kill a Mockingbird is narrated from the perspective of
options: Atticus Finch, her father
Scout Finch, a young girl reflecting on her childhood
Boo Radley, the reclusive neighbour
Tom Robinson, the falsely accused man
questions.explanation: The novel is narrated by Jean Louise 'Scout' Finch, recalling and reflecting on events from her childhood in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In To Kill a Mockingbird, Atticus Finch is a lawyer who defends
options: Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman
the reclusive neighbour, Boo Radley, in an unrelated matter
his own daughter, Scout, against false charges
Bob Ewell in a civil dispute
questions.explanation: Atticus Finch takes on the legally and socially difficult task of defending Tom Robinson, a Black man wrongly accused of a serious crime, in the racially prejudiced setting of the American South.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A major theme explored in To Kill a Mockingbird is
options: racial injustice and moral growth in a prejudiced society
international diplomacy between rival nations
space exploration and scientific advancement
the benefits of urban industrialisation
questions.explanation: The novel powerfully explores themes of racial prejudice, injustice, and the moral development of children (Scout and Jem) as they witness these realities in their community.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The title 'To Kill a Mockingbird' relates symbolically to the idea that
options: it is a sin to harm innocent, harmless beings who do no wrong, such as Tom Robinson and Boo Radley
mockingbirds are dangerous pests that must be eliminated
hunting birds is a celebrated tradition in Maycomb
Atticus Finch is himself literally a bird hunter
questions.explanation: The mockingbird symbolises innocent characters (notably Tom Robinson and Boo Radley) who are harmed despite doing nothing but good, reflecting the novel's central moral concern.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Boo Radley, a significant character in To Kill a Mockingbird, is initially portrayed to the children as
options: Scout's teacher at school
a mysterious, reclusive neighbour who is the subject of local rumours and fear
Atticus Finch's law partner
the town's respected mayor
questions.explanation: Boo Radley is initially depicted as a frightening, mysterious figure in local legend, though he is later revealed to be a gentle, protective presence in the children's lives.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: At the end of To Kill a Mockingbird, Tom Robinson is
options: acquitted and freed by the jury
never brought to trial at all
convicted by the all-white jury despite clear evidence of his innocence, and is later killed while attempting to escape prison
found to have committed the crime after new evidence emerges
questions.explanation: Despite Atticus's compelling defence and clear evidence pointing to his innocence, Tom Robinson is convicted by the prejudiced jury, and is later shot and killed while attempting to escape custody.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Path of Lucas: The Journey He Endured, an alternative non-African prose text on the JAMB syllabus, was written by
options: Susanne Bellefeuille
Pede Hollist
Harper Lee
Elma Shaw
questions.explanation: Path of Lucas: The Journey He Endured is a novel by Susanne Bellefeuille, offered as an alternative non-African prose text alongside To Kill a Mockingbird on the harmonized syllabus.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: As suggested by its title, Path of Lucas: The Journey He Endured centrally concerns
options: an adventure story set entirely in outer space
a historical account of European colonisation
a purely comedic tale with no serious themes
the personal struggles and journey of endurance faced by its central character, Lucas
questions.explanation: As the title indicates, the novel follows the difficult personal journey and hardships endured by its central character, Lucas, a theme reflected directly in the book's title.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Which of the following is a shared thematic concern between To Kill a Mockingbird and Path of Lucas, as non-African prose texts on the syllabus?
options: A focus purely on light-hearted, comedic events with no deeper meaning
The celebration of unchecked wealth and material success
The endurance of hardship and the pursuit of moral growth or justice
The complete absence of any central conflict
questions.explanation: Both novels, in their own settings, explore characters enduring significant hardship while grappling with questions of justice, resilience, and moral development.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'Once Upon a Time' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Syl Cheney-Coker
Gabriel Okara
Wole Soyinka
Niyi Osundare
questions.explanation: 'Once Upon a Time' is a well-known poem by the Nigerian poet Gabriel Okara.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of Gabriel Okara's 'Once Upon a Time' is
options: the loss of genuine human sincerity and warmth in modern, sophisticated society
the celebration of technological progress
the joys of childhood without any deeper reflection
a description of a beautiful natural landscape
questions.explanation: The poem laments how people have become insincere and superficial in their social interactions ('laugh with their eyes while their ice-block-cold eyes search behind my shadow'), contrasting this with a more genuine past.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In 'Once Upon a Time', the speaker expresses a desire to
options: travel to a foreign country permanently
forget his own children completely
become wealthier than his neighbours
relearn how to laugh and be genuinely sincere, as he once was as a child
questions.explanation: The poem's speaker, addressing his son, wishes to unlearn the artificial habits of adulthood and rediscover the genuine, unguarded sincerity he had as a child.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'New Tongue' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Wole Soyinka
Elizabeth L.A. Kamara
Niyi Osundare
S.O.H. Afriyie-Vidza
questions.explanation: 'New Tongue' is a poem by the Sierra Leonean poet Elizabeth L.A. Kamara, included on the harmonized JAMB Literature syllabus.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'Night' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Syl Cheney-Coker
Gabriel Okara
Niyi Osundare
Wole Soyinka
questions.explanation: 'Night' is a poem by the Nigerian Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka, exploring imagery and reflection associated with the night.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'Not My Business' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Elizabeth L.A. Kamara
Wole Soyinka
Gabriel Okara
Niyi Osundare
questions.explanation: 'Not My Business' is a well-known poem by the Nigerian poet Niyi Osundare.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of Niyi Osundare's 'Not My Business' is
options: the beauty of a rural farming landscape
the joys of international travel
the danger of indifference to injustice suffered by others, since it may eventually affect oneself
a celebration of a wedding ceremony
questions.explanation: The poem uses a repeated refrain of persecuted neighbours to warn against complacent indifference to injustice, since the speaker ultimately becomes a victim themselves.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'Hearty Garlands' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: S.O.H. Afriyie-Vidza
Syl Cheney-Coker
Wole Soyinka
Gabriel Okara
questions.explanation: 'Hearty Garlands' is a poem by S.O.H. Afriyie-Vidza, included among the prescribed African poems on the harmonized JAMB Literature syllabus.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'The Breasts of the Sea' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Gabriel Okara
Niyi Osundare
Syl Cheney-Coker
Wole Soyinka
questions.explanation: 'The Breasts of the Sea' is a poem by the Sierra Leonean poet Syl Cheney-Coker, featured on the harmonized JAMB Literature syllabus.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Which of the following poets on the JAMB African poetry list is a Nigerian Nobel Laureate in Literature?
options: Wole Soyinka
Niyi Osundare
Gabriel Okara
Syl Cheney-Coker
questions.explanation: Wole Soyinka, author of 'Night', won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, becoming the first African laureate in the category.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Gabriel Okara, the poet of 'Once Upon a Time', is notable in African literature for his
options: experimentation with translating Ijaw speech rhythms and thought patterns into English poetry and prose
work being set entirely outside Africa
exclusive focus on writing in French
career as primarily a playwright rather than a poet or novelist
questions.explanation: Okara, a Nigerian writer of Ijaw heritage, is well known for his stylistic innovation in rendering African linguistic patterns and thought structures into English literary form.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Which theme is commonly shared across several of the prescribed African poems, such as 'Once Upon a Time' and 'Not My Business'?
options: A detailed scientific description of natural phenomena
Social critique of dishonesty, indifference, or moral decline in society
The celebration of purely personal romantic love with no social commentary
An account of a historical military battle
questions.explanation: Both poems, in different ways, critique aspects of social behaviour — insincerity in 'Once Upon a Time' and dangerous indifference in 'Not My Business' — reflecting a broader trend of social critique in African poetry.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Elizabeth L.A. Kamara and Syl Cheney-Coker, two poets on the JAMB African poetry list, share a connection to which West African country?
options: Ghana
Sierra Leone
Nigeria
Senegal
questions.explanation: Both Elizabeth L.A. Kamara and Syl Cheney-Coker are poets connected to Sierra Leone, reflecting the syllabus's inclusion of a range of West African literary voices.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The recurring refrain technique, in which a phrase or line is repeated throughout a poem, is often used to
options: indicate the poem has no coherent structure
replace the need for a title
confuse the reader intentionally
reinforce a central theme or emotional emphasis
questions.explanation: Poets frequently use refrains (repeated lines or phrases) to reinforce key ideas, build rhythm, or intensify emotional impact, a technique seen in poems like 'Not My Business'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Poetic imagery, as used in the prescribed African poems, refers to the
options: number of stanzas contained in the poem
poet's biographical background
use of vivid, descriptive language that appeals to the senses to create mental pictures
strict rhyme scheme followed throughout a poem
questions.explanation: Imagery involves language that evokes sensory experiences (sight, sound, touch, etc.), helping readers visualise and emotionally connect with the ideas expressed in a poem.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'She Walks in Beauty' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Wilfred Wilson Gibson
Lord Byron
Fleur Adcock
Geoffrey Chaucer
questions.explanation: 'She Walks in Beauty' is a celebrated poem by the English Romantic poet Lord Byron, admiring the beauty of a woman.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of Lord Byron's 'She Walks in Beauty' is
options: the celebration of scientific progress
the horrors of war
the poet's despair over unrequited love
the harmonious blend of physical beauty and inner goodness in the woman being described
questions.explanation: The poem praises a woman's beauty as a perfect balance of light and dark, external and internal, suggesting her physical loveliness reflects an inner peace and goodness.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'The Stone' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Lord Byron
Wilfred Wilson Gibson
Fleur Adcock
Geoffrey Chaucer
questions.explanation: 'The Stone' is a poem by the English poet Wilfred Wilson Gibson, often noted for its poignant treatment of grief and loss, particularly associated with the impact of war.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme explored in Wilfred Wilson Gibson's 'The Stone' is
options: grief and the emotional impact of losing a loved one
the beauty of a spring landscape
the excitement of travelling to a new city
a humorous depiction of everyday village life
questions.explanation: The poem centres on a poignant, understated conversation revealing a father's grief upon learning of the death of his son, exploring themes of loss and mourning.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: 'The Nun's Priest's Tale', a poem on the JAMB Literature syllabus, was written by
options: Lord Byron
Geoffrey Chaucer
Fleur Adcock
Wilfred Wilson Gibson
questions.explanation: 'The Nun's Priest's Tale' is one of the tales from Geoffrey Chaucer's 'The Canterbury Tales', a major work of medieval English literature.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: 'The Nun's Priest's Tale' is notable for being told using which literary device, featuring a rooster and a fox as central characters?
options: A modern free-verse structure with no rhyme or metre
A beast fable, using animal characters to convey a moral lesson
A purely factual historical account
A dramatic monologue delivered by a human king
questions.explanation: The tale is structured as a beast fable, featuring the rooster Chanticleer and a cunning fox, using their interactions to deliver moral and satirical commentary, in the tradition of Aesop's fables.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Geoffrey Chaucer, author of 'The Nun's Priest's Tale', is best known as a major figure in
options: medieval English literature, particularly through 'The Canterbury Tales'
twentieth-century modernist poetry
African oral storytelling traditions
Romantic-era English poetry
questions.explanation: Chaucer, often called the 'father of English literature', is renowned for 'The Canterbury Tales', a collection of stories written in Middle English in the late 14th century.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poem 'The Telephone Call' on the JAMB Literature syllabus was written by
options: Lord Byron
Wilfred Wilson Gibson
Fleur Adcock
Geoffrey Chaucer
questions.explanation: 'The Telephone Call' is a poem by the New Zealand-born poet Fleur Adcock.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A central theme of Fleur Adcock's 'The Telephone Call' is
options: the excitement and subsequent disappointment or deception experienced by the speaker over unexpected news
the celebration of a national holiday
the joys of a long, happy marriage
an account of a historical battle
questions.explanation: The poem follows the speaker's rising excitement upon receiving apparently good news over the phone, only for this excitement to be undercut by disappointment, often interpreted as a satire on false promises like sweepstake scams.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the difference in poetic tradition between Lord Byron's Romantic poetry and Geoffrey Chaucer's medieval poetry?
options: Byron's poetry always uses animal characters, exactly like Chaucer's 'The Nun's Priest's Tale'
Chaucer's work has no relationship at all to storytelling or narrative
Byron's Romantic poetry emphasises individual emotion and idealised beauty, while Chaucer's medieval work often uses allegory and moral storytelling within a broader social frame
Byron wrote exclusively in Middle English, while Chaucer wrote in modern English
questions.explanation: Byron represents the Romantic era's focus on intense personal feeling and idealised beauty, while Chaucer's medieval storytelling often blends allegory, humour, and moral instruction within a wider narrative frame like 'The Canterbury Tales'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Unlike the other prescribed non-African poems, which are shorter lyric or narrative poems, 'The Nun's Priest's Tale' is distinct in that it
options: was written in the twenty-first century
forms part of a larger, extended collection of interlinked tales
is the shortest poem on the entire syllabus
contains no characters of any kind
questions.explanation: Unlike the standalone shorter poems by Byron, Gibson, and Adcock, Chaucer's tale is one part of the much larger framed narrative collection, 'The Canterbury Tales'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Tragicomedy, as a dramatic genre, is best defined as a play that
options: combines elements of both tragedy and comedy, often averting a fully tragic outcome despite serious themes and potential disaster
is a serious tragedy performed purely for comic relief
contains no serious themes whatsoever
is identical to farce in tone and structure
questions.explanation: Tragicomedy blends serious, potentially tragic material with elements of comedy, frequently steering the plot away from a fully disastrous conclusion, unlike pure tragedy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Melodrama, as a dramatic form, is distinguished from tragedy chiefly by its
options: total absence of any conflict
reliance on exaggerated emotion, sensational plotting, and clear-cut moral polarities rather than complex tragic causation
exclusive use of blank verse
setting always in ancient Greece
questions.explanation: Melodrama favours heightened emotion, sensational incident, and simple moral contrasts between good and evil, lacking the complex causation and psychological depth typical of tragedy.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Farce is best characterised by
options: profound philosophical reflection on mortality
a single tragic hero undone by hubris
improbable situations, exaggerated physical comedy, and rapid, chaotic plot complications played for broad laughter
a chorus commenting on the moral action
questions.explanation: Farce relies on absurd, improbable scenarios, slapstick physical comedy, and fast-paced misunderstandings purely for broad comic effect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: As a literary mode, satire primarily aims to
options: evoke pity and fear in the audience
provide purely factual historical record
create suspense through withheld information
ridicule or expose human vice, folly, or societal shortcomings, often with a view to reform
questions.explanation: Satire uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to criticise human weaknesses or societal problems, often with an implicit aim of prompting change.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The key distinction between a soliloquy and a monologue is that a soliloquy is
options: delivered by a character alone (or believing themselves alone) on stage, whereas a monologue is an extended speech addressed to other characters present
always in verse, while a monologue is always in prose
delivered only by villains
shorter than a monologue
questions.explanation: A soliloquy reveals private thoughts with no other characters presumed to be listening, while a monologue is a long uninterrupted speech delivered to other characters within the scene.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Unlike a soliloquy, a dramatic aside is typically
options: delivered while the character is completely alone on stage
a brief remark directed at the audience while other characters remain on stage, unheard by them
sung rather than spoken
reserved for the play's final scene
questions.explanation: An aside is a short comment shared with the audience even as other characters remain present on stage, distinguishing it from a soliloquy delivered in solitude.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Dramatic irony differs from situational irony in that dramatic irony depends on
options: an outcome that contradicts expectations shared by both characters and audience alike
the use of sarcasm in dialogue
a gap between what the audience knows and what a character on stage knows, whereas situational irony involves a contrast between expected and actual outcomes regardless of audience knowledge
events that could never plausibly occur
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony specifically requires the audience to possess knowledge a character lacks, while situational irony concerns a general mismatch between expectation and outcome.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Verbal irony occurs when
options: a character's fate is worse than expected by the audience
an unforeseen twist alters the plot's direction
a chorus foretells future events
a speaker says something that means the opposite of, or diverges from, their literal words
questions.explanation: Verbal irony arises when what is said differs from, or contradicts, what is actually meant, often for sarcastic or humorous effect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A foil, as a character device, functions primarily to
options: highlight particular qualities of another character (often the protagonist) through deliberate contrast
narrate events the protagonist cannot witness
resolve the plot's central conflict directly
provide comic relief exclusively
questions.explanation: A foil is a character whose contrasting traits or choices throw the qualities of another character into sharper relief.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Comic relief in an otherwise serious or tragic play serves to
options: eliminate all tension for the remainder of the play
briefly ease audience tension through humour before the seriousness of the plot resumes
replace the play's climax entirely
reveal the tragic hero's hamartia
questions.explanation: Comic relief provides a temporary release from mounting dramatic tension without permanently altering the play's serious trajectory.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Whereas exposition introduces the background, characters, and setting at a play's opening, the denouement refers to the
options: rising complication of the plot's central conflict
turning point at which the protagonist's fortune changes
final resolution or unravelling of the plot's complications after the climax
formal division of a play into acts
questions.explanation: The denouement is the concluding stage of a plot, in which loose ends are resolved following the climax, in contrast to the opening exposition.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The climax of a dramatic plot refers to
options: the introductory background information given at the start
the concluding resolution of all remaining conflicts
a secondary, unrelated subplot
the point of highest tension or the turning point in the conflict, after which events move toward resolution
questions.explanation: The climax marks the peak of dramatic tension and the decisive turning point after which the plot moves toward its resolution.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A play or narrative that begins 'in medias res' is one that
options: opens in the middle of the action, with earlier events later revealed through exposition or flashback
begins strictly at the chronological start of the story
has no discernible plot structure
is narrated entirely in the future tense
questions.explanation: 'In medias res' means 'into the middle of things', a technique where the narrative opens partway through the action rather than at its chronological beginning.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: 'Deus ex machina' refers to a plot device in which
options: the protagonist solves the conflict through careful long-term planning
an unexpected, often implausible force or event suddenly resolves a seemingly unsolvable conflict
the antagonist is revealed to be the narrator
two characters switch identities unexpectedly
questions.explanation: 'Deus ex machina' ('god from the machine') describes a sudden, often contrived resolution to a plot's conflict, historically inspired by gods being lowered onto the stage in Greek theatre.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The classical dramatic unities of action, time, and place, as codified from Aristotelian principles, require that a play
options: contain multiple unrelated subplots across many years
shift freely between numerous distant settings
confine its action to a single main plot, occurring within a single day, and set in a single location
always end tragically
questions.explanation: The classical unities call for a play to maintain one principal plot, unfold within roughly a single day, and remain in one location, for the sake of dramatic coherence.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In classical Greek drama, the chorus primarily functions to
options: serve as the play's central antagonist
replace dialogue between principal characters entirely
resolve the plot's conflict directly through action
comment on the action, provide background, and express communal or moral perspectives on events
questions.explanation: The chorus offers commentary, moral reflection, and context on the unfolding events, mediating between the action on stage and the audience.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Stage directions in a printed play script are best understood as
options: instructions describing setting, movement, gesture, or tone, intended to guide performance and reader interpretation without being spoken by characters
dialogue spoken directly to the audience
a form of soliloquy
footnotes added only by literary critics after publication
questions.explanation: Stage directions guide staging, movement, and delivery, providing information to performers and readers that is not spoken aloud as dialogue.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A comedy of manners is a form of comic drama that primarily satirises
options: supernatural events and ghosts
the affectations, manners, and social pretensions of a particular class or society
historical military conflicts
rural agricultural life
questions.explanation: A comedy of manners mocks the artificial behaviours, social customs, and pretensions of a particular social class, often through witty dialogue.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Which of the following best describes 'man versus society' as a form of dramatic conflict?
options: A struggle confined entirely within a single character's mind with no external consequence
A conflict between two natural forces such as storms
A protagonist's struggle against prevailing social norms, institutions, or collective values
A conflict resolved purely through comic misunderstanding
questions.explanation: 'Man versus society' conflict pits an individual's goals or values against the norms, institutions, or expectations of the wider community.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Aristotelian dramatic theory, 'anagnorisis' refers to the moment when
options: a chorus exits the stage
the setting shifts from day to night
comic relief is introduced
a character moves from ignorance to knowledge, recognising the truth about their situation or identity
questions.explanation: Anagnorisis is the critical moment of recognition in which a character discovers a crucial truth, often triggering or accompanying the play's reversal of fortune.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Unlike plays that strictly observe the classical unity of place, Antony and Cleopatra is notable for its
options: sweeping, episodic structure that shifts rapidly between numerous locations across the Roman and Egyptian worlds
confinement to a single room for the entire play
complete absence of any historical basis
use of a chorus to narrate all offstage action
questions.explanation: Shakespeare's play ranges widely across Rome, Egypt, and other locations, rejecting the classical unity of place in favour of an expansive, episodic structure suited to its political and geographical scope.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In Antony and Cleopatra, Enobarbus functions dramatically as
options: the play's tragic hero
an outsider-commentator whose blunt, worldly perspective offers the audience a more objective view of Antony and Cleopatra's relationship
Cleopatra's chief political rival
the sole comic relief character
questions.explanation: Enobarbus, as Antony's plain-spoken companion, provides an outsider's clear-eyed commentary on events, including his famous description of Cleopatra, giving the audience perspective beyond the central lovers' own viewpoints.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Antony's death after mistakenly believing Cleopatra has died exemplifies which literary device?
options: situational irony only, since the audience is equally deceived until that point
hyperbole
tragic/dramatic irony, since the audience recognises the misunderstanding that leads directly to Antony's fatal decision
comic relief
questions.explanation: Because the audience is aware the report of Cleopatra's death is false before Antony acts on it, his fatal decision carries the weight of dramatic irony.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A distinctive dramatic technique used in The Marriage of Anansewa, drawing on its storytelling roots, is the
options: strict adherence to a single unbroken continuous timeline
total absence of music or song
use of exclusively offstage violence
inclusion of song-and-dance interludes (Mboguo) and a storyteller-like narrator figure that breaks the fourth wall
questions.explanation: Efua Sutherland's play incorporates musical interludes and a narrator figure rooted in the Anansegoro storytelling tradition, engaging the audience directly in ways distinct from purely naturalistic drama.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The Common Man in A Man for All Seasons resembles the chorus of classical Greek drama in that both
options: address the audience directly and provide commentary that frames the audience's understanding of events
always remain silent throughout the performance
are individually named, complex tragic heroes
exist only in the play's final scene
questions.explanation: Like a classical chorus, the Common Man addresses the audience directly, offering framing commentary and perspective on the unfolding action throughout the play.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Thomas More's downfall in A Man for All Seasons is best understood not as the result of a tragic flaw in the Aristotelian sense but as the consequence of
options: a comic misunderstanding resolved happily
his unwavering moral integrity clashing irreconcilably with the political demands of the state
a fatal error in military judgement
an accidental crime he did not intend to commit
questions.explanation: Unlike heroes undone by a personal error or flaw, More's downfall stems directly from his principled refusal to compromise his conscience, placing him in irreconcilable conflict with the King's demands.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The final phone call announcing that a real inspector is on his way to the Birling household functions chiefly as
options: comic relief undercutting the play's serious tone
an unrelated subplot with no bearing on the main themes
a device that reintroduces suspense and reinforces the play's cyclical structure, implying the consequences of the family's actions are inescapable
evidence that Inspector Goole's investigation was entirely fabricated and irrelevant
questions.explanation: The closing twist restarts the cycle of investigation, suggesting that regardless of Inspector Goole's true identity, the family cannot escape accountability for their actions.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The contrasting reactions of the older Birlings and their children to Inspector Goole's revelations primarily serve to
options: prove that younger characters are always less intelligent than their elders
resolve the play's plot before its final act
introduce a romantic subplot unrelated to the main theme
highlight a generational divide between rigid self-interest and a growing capacity for social conscience and accountability
questions.explanation: Priestley contrasts the unrepentant older Birlings with Sheila and Eric's genuine remorse to dramatise a generational shift toward social responsibility.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: As alternative texts on the syllabus, Once Upon an Elephant and The Marriage of Anansewa both exemplify African drama's tendency to
options: draw on indigenous oral traditions and cultural values as the basis for dramatic form and theme
reject any use of dialogue in favour of pure mime
be set exclusively in modern European cities
avoid any engagement with themes of tradition or heritage
questions.explanation: Both plays draw significantly on African cultural heritage and oral storytelling traditions in shaping their themes and dramatic structure.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Compared to the sweeping political and romantic tragedy of Antony and Cleopatra, A Man for All Seasons presents tragedy on a more
options: purely comic register with no serious consequence
intimate, personal scale, centred on one man's private conscience within a constrained historical setting
supernatural, otherworldly plane
chaotic, plotless structure
questions.explanation: Where Antony and Cleopatra spans empires and continents, A Man for All Seasons focuses tightly on one man's personal moral struggle against the state.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An Inspector Calls is often described as a 'morality play' in modern dress because it
options: is set entirely in a church
contains no named characters
uses an investigative plot to dramatise ethical lessons about collective social responsibility, similar to how medieval morality plays taught moral lessons through allegory
was written in Middle English
questions.explanation: The play's investigative structure serves an underlying didactic purpose, teaching a lesson about social responsibility much as medieval morality plays used allegorical figures to instruct audiences.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Cleopatra, as presented in Antony and Cleopatra, is best described as a
options: flat character defined by a single unchanging trait
minor character with negligible influence on the plot
purely villainous antagonist with no redeeming qualities
round, complex character whose contradictory moods and 'infinite variety' resist simple categorisation
questions.explanation: Cleopatra is portrayed with striking psychological complexity and contradiction, famously described as possessing 'infinite variety', marking her as a fully round character.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Much of the comic tension in The Marriage of Anansewa arises from
options: dramatic irony, as the audience is aware of Ananse's scheme to court multiple suitors while the suitors themselves remain unaware
a tragic flaw leading to Ananse's death
the total absence of any conflict
a chorus that resolves the plot directly
questions.explanation: The audience's awareness of Ananse's simultaneous scheming with several suitors, unknown to those suitors, generates much of the play's comic dramatic irony.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The restrained, dignified tone of More's execution in A Man for All Seasons distinguishes the play's ending from
options: satire
melodrama, which would typically heighten the scene with exaggerated emotional excess
comedy
farce
questions.explanation: Bolt presents More's death with restraint and dignity rather than the exaggerated emotional excess characteristic of melodrama.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The recurring structural alternation between Roman and Egyptian settings in Antony and Cleopatra chiefly serves to
options: confuse the audience about the play's timeline
symbolically reinforce the central tension between disciplined political duty (Rome) and passionate excess (Egypt)
provide comic relief between serious scenes
demonstrate the unity of place
questions.explanation: The shifting settings mirror the play's thematic conflict between Roman discipline and duty and Egyptian passion and pleasure.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A third-person omniscient narrator, as distinct from a third-person limited narrator, is one who
options: narrates using 'I' throughout
can access only a single character's thoughts
never reveals any character's inner thoughts
has unrestricted access to the thoughts, feelings, and motivations of multiple or all characters in the story
questions.explanation: An omniscient narrator can move freely between the minds of different characters, unlike a limited narrator confined to one character's perspective.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An unreliable narrator is best defined as a narrator whose
options: credibility is compromised, such that readers must question the accuracy or honesty of their account
account is always entirely factual
identity is never revealed
narration occurs exclusively in verse
questions.explanation: An unreliable narrator's version of events may be distorted by bias, limited knowledge, deception, or naivety, requiring readers to read critically rather than take the account at face value.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Stream of consciousness, as a narrative technique, seeks to represent
options: a strictly chronological retelling of external events only
the continuous, often unstructured flow of a character's thoughts, feelings, and impressions as they occur
a dialogue exclusively between two characters
an omniscient narrator's moral judgement on events
questions.explanation: Stream of consciousness attempts to mirror the natural, often fragmented flow of a character's inner mental experience.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An epistolary novel is a work of fiction structured primarily through
options: a single continuous first-person confession
dramatic dialogue with stage directions
letters, diary entries, or other documents exchanged or written by its characters
rhymed verse stanzas
questions.explanation: Epistolary novels tell their story through a collection of documents such as letters or diary entries, rather than conventional continuous narration.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A 'bildungsroman' is a type of novel that centres on
options: a detective's investigation of a crime
a chorus commenting on events
an epic battle between nations
the psychological and moral growth of its protagonist from youth to maturity
questions.explanation: A bildungsroman traces a protagonist's formative development and moral or psychological maturation, often from childhood or adolescence into adulthood.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A narrative told in the second-person point of view is distinguished by its use of
options: 'you' to address the reader or a character as though they were the one experiencing the events
'I' throughout to denote the narrator as a participant
'he' and 'she' exclusively
an entirely dialogue-based structure with no narration
questions.explanation: Second-person narration directly addresses 'you', positioning the reader (or an addressed character) as the one undergoing the narrated events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An allegory differs from the isolated use of symbolism in that an allegory
options: never contains any hidden or secondary meaning
sustains a coherent secondary layer of meaning throughout an entire narrative, with characters and events systematically representing abstract ideas
is only found in poetry
always exaggerates events for comic effect
questions.explanation: While symbolism may involve isolated symbolic objects or images, allegory sustains a complete, systematic correspondence between a narrative's elements and abstract ideas throughout the work.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Indirect characterisation, as opposed to direct characterisation, reveals a character's traits through
options: an explicit authorial statement naming the trait outright
a glossary at the end of the novel
the character's actions, speech, thoughts, and other characters' reactions, requiring the reader to infer their qualities
footnotes provided by the editor
questions.explanation: Indirect characterisation requires readers to infer personality traits from behaviour, dialogue, and the responses of others, rather than through direct authorial statement.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Freytag's pyramid, used to analyse narrative structure, identifies the stages of a plot as
options: prologue, chorus, epilogue only
hamartia, anagnorisis, catharsis
protasis, epitasis, catastrophe exclusively
exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution (denouement)
questions.explanation: Freytag's pyramid maps narrative structure through the five stages of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and denouement.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A motif, as distinct from a theme, refers to
options: a recurring element, image, or idea that reinforces and helps develop the work's broader theme
the single central message of the entire work
the narrator's personal opinion
the physical setting of the novel
questions.explanation: A motif is a recurring device or image within a work that supports and develops its overarching theme, rather than being the central message itself.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In much African prose fiction engaging with colonialism, a recurring narrative concern is the
options: glorification of colonial administration without critique
tension between indigenous cultural values and the disruptive imposition of foreign systems of governance, religion, or education
complete absence of any historical context
exclusive focus on European settings
questions.explanation: African prose fiction dealing with colonialism frequently explores the friction between indigenous traditions and imposed foreign institutions and values.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: When a novel's outcome directly contradicts what readers and characters alike had reasonably expected, this exemplifies
options: verbal irony
dramatic irony exclusively
situational irony
hyperbole
questions.explanation: Situational irony arises when actual outcomes diverge sharply from what was reasonably expected by both characters and readers.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Beyond merely establishing time and place, a novel's setting can function symbolically to
options: replace the need for characters altogether
serve solely as decorative background with no thematic function
list secondary characters only
reflect or reinforce the psychological, social, or thematic dimensions of the narrative
questions.explanation: A skilfully used setting can mirror or reinforce a story's underlying themes and the psychological or social states of its characters, beyond mere physical backdrop.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Flashback and foreshadowing are best distinguished by the fact that
options: flashback interrupts the narrative to present earlier events, while foreshadowing hints at events yet to come
both refer to identical techniques with different names
foreshadowing is used only in poetry
flashback always occurs at a novel's very end
questions.explanation: Flashback moves the narrative backward to earlier events, while foreshadowing points forward, hinting at what is yet to occur.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An author's distinctive 'style' in prose fiction is shaped primarily by elements such as
options: the cover design and font used in the print edition
diction, sentence structure, tone, and figurative language characteristic of that writer
the price of the book
the publisher's marketing strategy
questions.explanation: Authorial style is defined by recurring choices in word choice, sentence construction, tone, and use of figurative language, distinguishing one writer's voice from another's.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The narration of To Kill a Mockingbird is distinctive in that it combines
options: a purely detached third-person omniscient perspective
an unreliable narrator whose account cannot be trusted at all
a child's immediate perceptions with the retrospective, more mature understanding of the adult narrator looking back
multiple alternating first-person narrators
questions.explanation: Scout narrates as an adult recalling her childhood, blending a child's immediate impressions with the reflective insight of her older narrating self.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The mockingbird symbol recurs across the novel in relation to both Tom Robinson and Boo Radley, functioning as a
options: purely decorative detail with no thematic significance
literal warning about hunting regulations
device unrelated to the novel's title
unifying motif reinforcing the theme of destroying innocence
questions.explanation: The mockingbird recurs as a unifying symbol for harmless, innocent figures who are harmed despite doing no wrong, tying together the fates of Tom Robinson and Boo Radley.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A novel exploring the lasting psychological impact of a traumatic event on its protagonist, such as So the Path Does Not Die, often relies structurally on
options: flashback or non-linear time shifts to juxtapose past trauma with the protagonist's present circumstances
a strictly future-tense narrative voice
an entirely comic tone throughout
the complete omission of the protagonist's inner life
questions.explanation: Novels dealing with lasting trauma frequently use flashback or non-chronological structuring to connect a protagonist's past experiences to their present psychological state.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The title Redemption Road functions symbolically, using the image of a 'road' to suggest
options: a literal street map of Monrovia
a journey or process toward healing and moral or communal restoration, rather than a single fixed destination
a purely geographical description with no thematic weight
the author's own travel itinerary
questions.explanation: The 'road' in the title symbolises an ongoing journey toward healing and reconciliation, rather than a literal or purely descriptive geographical reference.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: In evaluating narrative technique across prescribed African prose texts dealing with social trauma, examiners typically expect candidates to identify
options: only the number of chapters in each novel
the price and publication date of each edition
